t: Why Granting a Favor Makes You Like People More
q: People generally believe they must feel warmth and connection before choosing to help someone. Liking people before agreeing to help them seems like the natural order of things. But the opposite is also true.

After doing someone a favor, people begin to like the other party more, even if they felt indifferent about them beforehand. This phenomenon is often termed the Ben Franklin Effect because he wrote about using small requests to soften his political rivals.” “The logic behind this effect is straightforward. People don not generally help others they dislike, so if they agree to a small request or favor, they reason they must like them after all. The need to align our beliefs and actions is a powerful force.

Leaders like people more who ask them for their advice and seek their feedback. The leader will often feel prideful for the other person's success. This is why mentors, coaches, and leaders often feel more deeply connected and committed to those who actively seek their guidance.

Leaders who ask team members to help them in various small projects, initiatives, and tasks give them the attention they crave. The more these requests are seen as doing the leader a favor, rather than complying with a directive, the more connection team members feel.

Granting small favors helps to build rapport, trust, and likability for both leaders and team members. People feel more connected when they are asked to contribute, especially to requests that seem personal and confidential.

Thoughtful favors that signal respect and show a genuine interest in others are best, of course. Requesting an introduction, asking for advice, seeking a ride, validating an idea, requesting a check or edit, thinking through a decision, and soliciting a demonstration are common examples.
This effect flips our assumption about generosity. We don't just help people we like. We start liking the people we help.” Archived from Admired Leadership on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

t: More Challenges To Church-State Wall Coming To Schools
q: In May of this year, the Supreme Court ended the hope that an Oklahoma Catholic charter school would be first in the nation to shatter the wall between religion and public schools. Now two schools are poised to challenge the notion that a public charter school must be non-sectarian.

On November 3, Peter Deutsch submitted a letter of intent to apply for charter authorization to the Oklahoma Statewide Charter School Board (the same board that previously approved St. Isidore), as reported by Nuria Martinez-Keel at Oklahoma Voice.

Deutsch, a representative of the National Ben Gamla Jewish Charter School Foundation, previously founded a chain of Ben Gamla non-religious Hebrew-English charter schools in Florida. The proposed school would be their first school outside of Florida.
Local Jewish leaders say they were blindsided by the proposal and argue that such a school is not needed. But approval does not appear to be the real goal here.

Eric Baxter, vice-president and general counsel at Becket, a leading religious-liberty law firm that is representing Ben Gamla, said we would represent Ben Gamla challenging that decision in the federal courts in Oklahoma. Becket boasts an unparalleled, undefeated record at the Supreme Court.

Ben Gamla schools are actually run by Academica, a Florida for-profit charter management organization that provides facilities, finance, staffing and human resource coordination, as well as bookkeeping, budgeting, regulatory compliance and financial forecasting.

According to the letter of intent, the proposed school would provide Oklahoma's state-approved academic standards alongside Jewish religious studies, enabling students to achieve college readiness while developing deep Jewish knowledge, faith, and values within a supportive learning community.

As Ben Gamla is proposing almost exactly what St. Isidore offered, it seems very likely that the Oklahoma supreme court would rule against them, thereby setting up a federal challenge.” Archived from Curmudgucation (Substack, originally Forbes.com) on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

t: The Wrongness Tax
q: You're wrong about something important right now. You've probably known for a while. Maybe months. Maybe longer. There's a belief you hold, a position you've defended, a decision you've justified that doesn't quite hold up anymore.
The evidence has been accumulating. The cracks are showing.
But you haven't admitted it yet. You're waiting for the right moment. A moment when admitting it won't cost as much.
That moment never comes. Every day you wait, the cost goes up.
The longer you carry a false position, the more you have to reconstruct when you finally let it go.
Your credibility, trust with others, and your own clarity all suffer when you maintain a false position longer than necessary.” Archived from Scott D. Clary Newsletter on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

t: The Language of Belonging
q: If you were not worried about belonging before the new Ofsted framework, you are now. The new inspection toolkit defines belong as one of three core lenses through which inspectors will evaluate a school.

Under the 2025 framework, inclusion, with belonging folded into it, becomes a discrete area of evaluation. Inspectors expect schools to show how they notice and respond to those who meet resistance in the system.

Most writing about belonging treats it as a kind of emotional weather system that drifts over children and shapes their commitment to school. As long we focus, so the logic goes, on warm relationships, smiles in corridors and signals of care all will be well.
This absence is odd because the lived experience of school, and every other aspect of life, is linguistic from start to finish. To belong is to feel able to take part in its conversations.
The corridors are thick with talk, and much of that talk is academic in character. It has a grammar, a cadence and a set of tacit assumptions. You either understand or you do not.

Yet for all its impressive scope, the study also exposes the blind spot that runs through almost the entire field. It tracks social bonds, perceptions of care and the sense that adults in school notice what children do.

Now, I would go further: To be academically successful, children need not just to be fluent in the language of academic success, but to recognize themselves as belonging within the communities that use it.” Archived from David Didau on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

t: Do You Watch Too Many Revenge Films?
q: Thoughts of revenge can channel complex emotions, anger, grief, humiliation, and power, into a controlled narrative with closure. The idea of exacting revenge restores feelings of agency and control and amplifies feelings of empowerment.

People are drawn to fictional stories of revenge because they evoke primal feelings of justice, catharsis, and power over enemies and threats. Watching or reading stories where victims are transformed into avengers helps the audience examine their own relationship between power and empathy.

Unlike real life, the conflict is resolved permanently, and the sense of order that the real world often denies is reaffirmed. Unfortunately, repeated exposure to revenge narratives has been shown to heighten moral polarization and desensitize empathy.

Leaders who expose themselves to a steady diet of revenge movies and books are more likely to normalize grievance, see conflicts through an us versus them lens, and become subtly more aggressive and punitive in their behavior over time.
The risk is not that fictional stories reinforce bad instincts, but that repeated exposure trains a leader's internal script for how power, justice, and respect are to be handled.

Good leaders do not seek revenge. They recognize that retaliatory behavior is a personal, emotional, and backward-looking reaction. They know that what in the moment feels like righteous payback commonly exacerbates conflict and results in incivility and countermeasures.

When team members witness a leader engage in retaliatory behavior or reprisal, they view them as less trustworthy, more unfair, and highly unethical, no matter how justified the action may appear at the moment.

Accountability is corrective and forward-looking, while revenge is punitive and past-focused. Accountability is about establishing standards and elevating long-term performance, while revenge is about settling a score and inflicting pain.” Archived from Admired Leadership on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

t: Why ChatGPT for Teachers Might Make Things Worse
q: There’s a predictable pattern when some edtech companies enter education: they build sophisticated solutions to problems that don’t exist while ignoring the problems real teachers actually face.

The notion that students can be taught “general critical thinking skills” to evaluate AI outputs represents a profound misunderstanding of how critical thinking actually works. Critical thinking is not a portable skill that operates independently of domain knowledge, it is the product of domain expertise.

When you decompose a historical period into disconnected “facts” about dates and events, you lose the causal relationships, the narrative coherence. When you break a poem into atomic elements like “metaphor,” “imagery,” and “tone,” you end up feature-spotting and destroy the aesthetic encounter that gives literature its power.

We know from decades of research that retrieval practice, spaced repetition, and interleaving produce robust learning gains. We know that there’s an optimal difficulty zone. We know that spacing intervals should dynamically adjust based on individual mastery.

The problem isn’t knowing these principles work; it’s implementing them with precision for thirty students simultaneously across multiple topics over an entire academic year. This is exactly the kind of coordination puzzle at which AI excels and humans struggle.

The issue isn’t just that ChatGPT for Teachers solves the wrong problems; it’s that in doing so, it may make the right problems (such as implementing what we actually know about how learning happens), even harder to solve.

t: What Do We Mean When We Say "Times"?
q: In training sessions, I regularly ask attendees to draw a picture to represent “three times seven.” Every single time, I get back two different images. Some people draw three lots of seven. Others draw seven lots of three.

If I said “seven three times,” it feels much clearer: I mean three lots of seven (the red counters above). So perhaps that’s the issue. Maybe the problem lies not in the word itself but when we say it?

Because the structure of the maths still matters. Understanding whether we mean "three lots of seven" or "seven lots of three" helps children develop a deeper understanding -- especially once we move into division.
It goes on to say that “multiplied by” and “times by” are not used as this implies the multiplicand (the group size) is written first followed by the multiplier (the number of groups).
But do your staff know this? Can you aim for an agreed decision to avoid confusion? Definitely something to keep in mind for all the times that you say "times".

q: I am excited to see how this ‘first experiment’ works across different schools and subjects, and I need your help to make the definitive version even better.

Share the Power: If you find this useful, share the gem with colleagues, both in and outside your school, across any subject.

In the past, I would have used perhaps 20-30% of the teaching ideas and atoms the Gem suggested. Now, the planning is so precise, I am regularly using most of the atoms and teaching ideas it produces.

Human Expertise is Key: Not every lesson plan the Gem produces is perfect. Your expert judgment, your knowledge of your class, the common misconceptions, and the specific curriculum nuance, is essential. The Gem provides a robust super-scaffold for planning, but the teacher remains the architect.

t: The Lie About Guilt We Don't Question in Business
q: We mistake feeling guilty for being good. Especially in business.
Guilt didn’t make me show up better. It made me disappear. It made me hesitant.
Guilt is a spotlight. And the spotlight is pointed inward. It doesn’t fix the situation.
It just keeps you in a loop where everything is about your feelings instead of the responsibility in front of you.
If someone on your team came to you with the same mistake you’re punishing yourself for… would you forgive them?
What if guilt isn’t proof you’re a good person or a good leader? What if it’s a way of avoiding becoming the person the next chapter requires?

t: The Importance of Being Sincere
q: In an insincere society, everything and everyone is up for suspicion and scorn.
The ability to disagree affably is a supreme virtue, to disagree with your opponent precisely and carefully and even forcefully and yet gracefully.
We fall into this fallacy all the time in the contemporary world, a suspicion of our neighbor’s motives which distracts us from his or her arguments.
We should be able to say, “I think you are deeply wrong, but I understand how you came to your position.
Suspicion may be the death of us as a culture. And A.I. is only accelerating this problem.
A society of individuals who can disagree while understanding each other can negotiate and navigate challenges together, not perfectly, but possibly, with sacrifice.

Your peace of mind is worth more than your need to be right. The art of not being rattled is about the gap between the stimulus and your response. In that gap lies your freedom.” Archived from Scott D. Clary Newsletter on April 20, 2026 by Tim.

q: Backward design flips this approach, reversing the order so the end result is less accidental.

It’s honestly a pretty straightforward methodology because it demands conceptual clarity before instructional choices, which ensures the learning experience is driven by learning goals rather than instructor preferences, conveniences, or habits.

t: If We Don't Build Boyhood Spaces, the Internet Will
q: But subtraction is only half the equation. You also have to add something.
Boys need environments that challenge them and give them direction. They need chances to take risks, struggle, fail, and try again.

Take away real mentors, and boys find digital ones. Take away real challenges, and boys chase artificial ones. Take away real community, and boys latch onto whatever online tribe offers the clearest identity.
Male-centered spaces - healthy, structured, guided spaces - aren’t luxuries. They’re shock absorbers.
Boys don’t become good men accidentally. They need structure, they need guidance, and they need adults who are capable of exhibiting responsible masculinity.
Because if we don’t, the screen will raise them for us. And it won’t raise them well.

t: Be Careful Not to Weaponize Gratitude
q: When used as a directive, rather than as an expression, gratitude can be highly coercive.
Telling people they should be grateful chills dissent and legitimate concerns and complaints while dissuading people from challenging the status quo.
Any time people are told to be grateful, they naturally feel guilt over expressing their concerns.
Gratitude is a voluntary moral emotion that can’t be directed without becoming an act of control instead.
Some leaders intentionally control others using this manipulative tactic, but most do it unconsciously to express their own frustration.
Good leaders resist this siren call and encourage gratefulness by modeling it, inviting it, and making it easy to express.

t: Warding Off Classroom AI
q: Simply forbidding it is as effective as was the banning of Cliff Notes or Wikipedia.
Trying to chase the chatbots away is simply not going to work. More than that, it is not going to help students grasp an education.
As I’ve now said many times, AI most easily rushes into places where humanity has already been hollowed out.

Modern ed reform, with its test-centric data-driven outcome-based approach has pushed us even further toward classrooms that are product-centered rather than human-centered. But if class is all about the product, then AI can produce those artifacts far faster and more easily than human students.
The key to an AI-resistant classroom is not a batch of preventative rules.
Planning the details of a unit is hard--but it gets much easier if you know why you are teaching the unit in the first place.

t: The Leader's Guide to Giving and Receiving Authentic Praise
q: By making an effort to show sincere appreciation for my work, these commissioners inspired me to work harder.
The thing about compliments is that context matters, as do tone and word choice. You can pay a lot of compliments, but if they’re perfunctory, people will come to resent them.
Inauthentic or transactional praise is worse than none at all. It’s confusing, manipulative, and demoralizing.
Sparse praise undermines confidence. Too frequent praise can seem perfunctory.
Don’t hold your compliments till the annual review or some awards ceremony. People thrive on prompt feedback, both praise and critique.
Heartfelt praise is a form of gratitude, which means it can have a profound effect on the leader who offers it as well as on the recipient.

t: The Best Gratitude Practice Isn't What You Think
q: Being thanked, valued, and appreciated has an oversized impact on how people feel about themselves, feel motivated to perform, and feel connected and trustful with others.
Gratitude works in four directions. People can give it. They can receive it. They can reflect on it. And they can witness it.
But recent research has shown these effects to be small or modest, even when practiced religiously.
Surprisingly, and somewhat counterintuitively, brain research confirms it is the witnessing of gratitude that produces the most significant advantages for well-being.
The big advantage, of course, is that you don’t have to wait for thanks or appreciation.
The best gratitude practice is not to reflect on what you are grateful for but to watch others receive appreciation or act altruistically.

t: The 5 Paradoxes Every Leader Must Learn to Live With
q: So what do great leaders do? They make expectations clear, they hold the bar high, and they let their team own the “how”.
Every time you “jump in” to help your team, your team loses the chance to learn and grow.
Letting go of doing doesn’t mean letting go of standards. It means raising others to meet them.
But you don’t really have those answers - all you have is the gray and the murky. You never have the ‘full’ data, or the ‘perfect’ formula.
But you can’t force trust with rules and reminders. The only way to gain trust is to earn it.
The best leaders I have met have conquered their ego, and that’s exactly what makes them great.

t: What School Doesn't Teach Young People About Their First Job
q: A good education is a wonderful thing. But the mechanisms inherent in the education system are poor preparation for the environment most young people move into after graduation.
Unlike those right or wrong answers in school, the young employee faces an environment of great ambiguity.
It would make no sense to mess up the midterms to do better on the final exam, but that is in many cases how achievement at work comes about.
It matters less that they are doing a good job and more that their boss THINKS they are doing a good job.
There’s no greater academic sin than stealing someone else’s answers or copying their work. But in the private sector, stealing is required.
At work, learning often resembles a series of errors. That will be uncomfortable for most A-students.

t: Tips for Living with Scrupulosity
q: scrupulosity is a subtype of OCD in which you obsessively agonize over a religious or moral (usually religious) doubt or uncertainty and compulsively try to “resolve” the doubt.
Probably the most important pieces of advice I can give is to treat scrupulosity as OCD, not as some special, spiritual doubt.
But my main point here is that treating scrupulosity as primarily a spiritual question that has to be resolved rather than a mental health condition is a part of the mental health condition.
in Titus 3:9, Paul tells Titus to “avoid foolish controversies,” and I think that’s what OCD questions really are.
Allowing thoughts to just be there and exist without you having to do something to fix them or solve them or figure them out is key to having peace.
Yes, we may have intrusive thoughts that cause us to doubt, but we can be confident that even while we are blown about by doubts, his love never wavers.

t: Reformster Nostalgia and New Old Mistakes
q: It’s not just that the ed reform movement became infected with Culture Panic. It’s that the Culture Panic crowd is, almost without exception, a bunch of very unserious people.
Fatigue? Simplistic? No, the reason that reform flagged was because it didn’t work.
Market competition is a terrible fit for education (see Greene’s Law-- the free market does not foster superior quality; the free market fosters superior marketing).
There isn’t a shred of evidence for that assertion, but in the meantime, we keep pretending that a single mediocre math and reading test tells us everything we need to know about education.
Did test scores go up for a while? Sure. I was there. They went up because we learned how to align the schools to the test. Not to the education-- to the test.
I think it’s more accurate to frame the sides as pro- and anti- public education, and pro-public education voices have always been in very short supply in the reform coalition.
But ed reform continually misses the viewpoint of the people who have to actually implement policy ideas.

t: Getting to ‘No’ Faster
q: There is nothing more frustrating or deflating than spending oodles of time and energy on a project or initiative only to have it negated in a few seconds by a leader who doesn’t agree.

All leaders have the decision rights to negate or reset a project after the work has been done. Good leaders rarely assert those rights, while more imperial leaders typically have a history of razing nearly completed projects.

Teams and team members have an obligation to seek the guidelines and criteria for success for any project and to check in early and often so as not to surprise a leader with a finished product that they decide at the last minute they can’t live with.
They collaborate with the leader to establish the kill criteria before initiating the work.
Having a leader redirect the work at an early stage is much preferable to having them negate the project when it nears its conclusion.
A “No” is hard enough for a team to hear, but it is excruciatingly painful when it comes at the end of considerable work.

overnight sleep significantly aids memory retention. Furthermore, exploratory findings suggest that this consolidation can be positively linked to a student's capacity for learning new material the next day

t: The Algorithmic Turn: The Emerging Evidence On AI Tutoring That's Hard to Ignore
q: These are mechanisms, and mechanisms can be mechanised. But teaching, in its fullest sense, is about more than optimising cognitive mechanisms. It is about what we value, who we hope our students become, what kind of intellectual culture we create.
Penrose asked whether consciousness can be computed. The evidence from AI tutoring suggests that instruction can be. But whether instruction and education are the same thing remains an open question.

We stand at an inflection point where the technology is here, it’s improving exponentially, and pretending otherwise won’t make it go away. The question is not whether AI will transform education; it clearly already is.
The question is whether we have the courage to design it around evidence and human flourishing, or whether we’ll simply let it happen to us.

John Keats wrote of the mind as possessing a ‘wreath’d trellis of a working brain’ an image of organic complexity that resists simple mechanism. Perhaps this is what we fear losing: not just the efficiency of human teachers, but the tangled, mysterious process by which one mind awakens another.

t: Mini-Whiteboards: A Long-Overdue Rant (and Love Letter)
q: After 15 years of teaching, I still can’t wrap my head around one thing: how anyone manages without mini-whiteboards. MWBs are simple, cheap, and incredibly powerful. Yet, despite all the blogs, videos, and training out there, they remain underused.
Why? Because they let you see, instantly, what every single pupil knows -- or doesn't. And in that moment, you can make real, informed decisions about your teaching.

You cold call a pupil -- they get it right. You cold call another -- also right. Your brain says: Brilliant- they've got it! The class begins independent practice. And then... as you circulate... mistake after mistake after mistake.
If pupils aren’t trained, MWBs become a chaotic nightmare of dried up pens, lost lids, missing boards and noisy transitions. We’re still working on this as part of our “agreed consistencies.

Mini-whiteboards remain one of the most powerful, underrated, and essential tools in the classroom -- truly the icing that holds your teaching together. And I genuinely don't know how we teach effectively without them.

With MWB's, you can see misconceptions, partial understandings, and the strategies pupils are using to solve problems. When you work out what's happening underneath the answers, you can shape what comes next in a far more targeted way.

t: Few Americans Question Use of Computers in Classroom Lessons November 19, 2025 room-lessons/
q: Buck believes that U.S. educators should be leery, even skeptical, of using computer devices in lessons, and that teachers and school districts should demand evidence from vendors such as Apple, Microsoft, and Google that their devices and software are “improving academic outcomes.

Note the four "shoulds" in the above paragraph. Yet, the fact of the matter is that the folks who sell computers and software seldom offer proof of effectiveness for the simple reason that they lack "clear evidence of efficacy of their products...." None. Nada. Zip.

These devices have become accepted much like public utilities such as electricity, water, and gas that consumers use daily and pay for monthly. They have become the warp-and-woof of daily life. They have become necessities.

No district administrator, teacher, or parent needs research evidence to justify buying a laptop, tablet, or mobile phone for their schools, classroom, or children just as no research evidence is needed to prove that one must eat to survive.
Today, using laptops and tablets in classroom lessons is as normal as saying the Pledge of Allegiance in the third grade and smelling Lysol in the school’s bathrooms.
Whether they accelerate, confound, or impede student learning, much less academic achievement, is largely unknown, remaining an unanswered question for 2026.

t: 3-Read Friday #91
q: I am the world’s biggest mini-whiteboard fan (I have a book about them). However, they are not without those challenges. In this blog, Anna confronts some of those challenges and shares some practical ways to overcome them.
We recently released our first paper on our collaboration with Google DeepMind, which explores supporting human tutors with AI hints, so AI tutoring is very much on my mind at the moment.
Carl takes a deep dive into the subject, highlighting key considerations for those designing or considering using the technology.

Larry highlights how the use of laptops, tablets and other digital devices in U.S. classrooms has become so normalised that very few teachers, administrators or parents question whether they actually improve learning outcomes.
Meaningful data showing improved academic achievement remains lacking. I see parallels with many of the schools I visit!

t: Knowing When It’s Time to Quit
q: walking away from an unattainable goal is not a failure but a crucial leadership skill for organizational effectiveness.
the difference between reactive quitting and strategic quitting . These are two very different catalysts.
These “kill” criteria, as decision-making expert Annie Duke likes to call them, help to signal when the goal or outcome is no longer attainable
Setting kill criteria at the start of a project, strategy, or investment transforms quitting from reactive to strategic.
Once it becomes clear that the outcome is too costly or unreachable, the best description for continued commitment is foolish.

t: Ten Keys to Great PD
q: As I approach the 20-year mark of my career in education, I've probably spent thousands of hours thinking about, experiencing, or leading professional development experiences. Lots of them have been…not so great. But some of them? Career-changing.

The most impactful PD book I've read has probably been Mike Schmoker's book Focus. The man is relentlessly repetitive on his three things schools can do to get better. The repetition works. It signals importance. It signals there's more to learn in the seemingly simple and fundamental things that are being repeated.

Writing is the most efficient means for transforming the human mind. This is why my students write so much, mostly in the provisional mode of writing. It's also why I write so much. It's impossible to multi-task while writing, so it forces concentration. Writing is exploratory. It is generative.

Listen, colleague: my work is all about these four words. If something I share with you today doesn't seem likely to both produce more learning and reduce stress, don't do it. You don't need one more thing to do unless it can meet both those criteria. I don't either.

Give me a thing to mindlessly check off a list, and you won't change me. Give me a tool to use that I understand and teach me to treat this tool like a learning experience, and now you might end up changing me.
The most efficient means to change the world is by changing human beings; human beings change very reliably when you shape the mind and put ideas into practice.

t: The Delicate Task of Assigning a Team Member’s Idea to Someone Else
q: in many cases, they lack the skills, experience, or talent to execute on their own idea.
Ideas have two distinct stages—origination and execution. Not everyone is good at both.
The feedback should begin with genuine praise for the idea and their role in producing it.
it is best to frame the decision around role fit and project needs rather than on personal shortcomings.
The outcome leaders hope for is for the originator to be mildly disappointed but not discouraged.

t: Take Projects Apart to Develop Delegation Skills
q: Fearing standards will drop if they don’t have direct oversight of a project or task, leaders often take the helm even when the best choice would be to delegate.
Delegation is how good leaders leverage their time and focus.
Most projects are made up of dozens of requisite actions and steps. The idea is to get comfortable delegating a small set of them.
Be sure to give those entrusted with the task your guidelines, standards, and insights.
Without the right strategy, does perfect project execution even matter? Learning to delegate isn’t just an imperative. It is a necessity.

t: Research Bite #45: Deployment of Teaching Assistants Guidance Report
q: This guidance report from the Education Endowment Foundation (EEF) offers comprehensive recommendations for optimising the deployment of teaching assistants (TAs) in mainstream schools.

It emphasises that TAs should supplement, rather than replace, direct teacher instruction, particularly for students needing extra support, including those with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND).
Teachers retain primary responsibility for the learning of all pupils, especially low-prior-attaining pupils and pupils with SEND.
there's a risk TAs might unintentionally hinder pupil independence or replace teacher instruction, leading to negative outcomes or over-reliance.
TAs should supplement – not replace – the teacher. This means that pupils who struggle most should spend at least as much time with the teacher as other pupils, if not more.

The document outlines five key recommendations: ensuring TAs facilitate access to high-quality teaching, promoting student independence through scaffolding, effectively delivering evidence-based interventions, preparing and training staff for TA deployment, and engaging all staff in the implementation process.

t: Leaders Who Overemphasize Compensation Create Mercenaries
q: Compensation is the most direct expression of value in the workplace.
When money means too much to people, they often become “coin-operated,” where their motivation to do anything is directly linked to the monetary reward
When money means too little, it robs people of their initiative, often leading to complacency and a disrespect for merit and productivity.
A healthy relationship with money means it is valued to create experiences, help other people, buy back time, and gain access to support.
People aren’t wealthy or the most productive until they enjoy the intrinsic rewards money can’t buy.

t: Great Leadership Development Plans Share Four Ingredients
q: Many plans rely too heavily on assessment and not enough on skill and knowledge development.
Study after study reveals that leaders credit experiences over every other form for their biggest advancements in leadership development.
Great plans make room for introductions, conversations, and dialogues with people they don’t presently talk with but need to.
Leaders in a succession protocol typically need more time and investment to be ready for the next role.
Great Leadership Development Plans prepare leaders for a future they can’t yet see.

t: Why I Want to Be the Most Boring Teacher in the Building
q: We've built this myth of the great teacher - the one who dazzles, performs, entertains. Always upbeat. Always engaging. But here's the truth the hallway observers don't see: the flash rarely sticks.

I thought fun meant effective. My classroom was loud, colorful, fast-moving. It looked impressive. But when I checked what students actually remembered days and weeks later, it was like watching a Snapchat story disappear.
Learning that lasts is built on often unpleasant friction: retrieval, reflection, feedback, and practice.
Predictability frees up working memory for actual thinking. It creates safety and rhythm. It tells students, this is a place where your brain works hard, not your emotions.
Boring means consistent. Boring means clear. Boring means evidence-based.
The one who teaches for learning over the long-term, not for applause in the short-term.

t: What To Say To A Parent Who Resists Your Classroom Management https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2025/11/14/parent-who-resists-classroom-management/
q: The reason is that the sun rises and sets upon their golden child.
If you agree to make special accommodations, all hope is lost. You’ll lose respect from your entire class and their behavior will disintegrate.
The key is bluntness. Say the words and let them carry your message unadorned. Don’t explain further or ease the weight of your words.
How the parent feels about your convictions isn’t your concern.
Just be sure to remain polite, professional, and firm in your belief that accountability for misbehavior is good for your students.
If you hem and haw and show uncertainty and weakness, then the parent will be emboldened to double-down on their complaints.

t: Loyalty Is a Consequence of Leadership
q: Of the many illustrations of a leader’s prowess, loyalty from those they lead is the crowning jewel.
Leaders who consistently give loyalty by protecting, defending, and supporting others, especially during difficult moments, often receive it in return.
team members are more loyal to those leaders they perceive as having a higher character .
People are loyal to leaders who hold similar values and a vision they find compelling.
Make the investment to create more loyalty. One loyal team member is worth a dozen talented colleagues.

t: Faultless Vocabulary Instruction: Guaranteeing Understanding with Structural Precision with-structural-precision
q: Teaching failures often aren’t student failures, they are instructional failures, which are fundamentally communication failures.
Instruction is faulty when the structural features of the examples allow for misinterpretation or misgeneralisation by the learner.
Keep your teacher wording identical each time. This constant signal highlights the constant feature (the sameness) across all the changing contexts (irrelevant variation).
To establish the rule, we must use juxtaposition: present the positive and its contrasting negative example immediately together. This focuses the learner’s attention on the flipping feature.
If your instruction was faultless, the learner will be able to generalise the concept by correctly applying the label to new, unlabelled examples.
This approach moves vocabulary teaching from tell and hope to structural design and guaranteed comprehension.

t: Can ChatGPT Catch Educational Neuromyths? What Teachers Should Know About Asking AI for Help November 3, 2025
q: Generative AI outperformed humans when asked to evaluate neuromyth statements directly with their error rates (26–27%) only about half of those of humans (40–60%).
Generative AI performed much worse when the same neuromyths were implicitly included in user-like teaching questions with error rates jumping to 51–66%.
The fix? Prompting them to correct unsupported assumptions reduced error rates significantly, often outperforming even the direct neuromyth-checking approach.

When your prompt implicitly contains a neuromyth, generative AI will try to be helpful and match your assumptions. This is known as sycophantic behaviour, aligning with the user’s beliefs rather than checking them.
Just adding the instruction correct unsupported assumptions led to a significant drop in neuromyth-related errors.
LLMs are not fact-checking machines by default. They’re communication tools trained to predict the next best word, not necessarily the next true word.

t: 3-Read Friday #90: Vocabulary Instruction, AI and Neuromyths, and Boring Teaching
q: Jake’s aim for this post is to translate the core principles of Englemann’s Theory of Instruction into plain, teachable moves when explicitly teaching words. The results are excellent.

This fascinating study finds that models such as Chat GPT outperform humans at identifying educational neuromyths (such as we only use 10% of our brain) when asked directly, but falter when such myths are implicitly included in everyday teaching questions.
A positive reflection on why being a boring teacher can actually mean being a really effective teacher.
Before we begin, you may want to check out my brand-new 16-part book series, The Tips for Teachers guide to. Book 8 on Diagnostic Questions is now available.
Here are three blog posts that I found interesting this week.

t: Learning From the Competition Can Make You Better
q: Competitors can be a source of learning, growth, and inspiration — if leaders let them be.
CEO Jim Farley admitted that he was “humbled” after engineers tore apart a Tesla Model 3 and several Chinese electric vehicles in 2022.
Ford learned it had to catch up to its competitors so the company could compete in the future.
It is less important to learn what the competitor is doing and more important to understand why .
The best leaders refrain from comparison and focus on learning instead.

t: How to Help Grade-Obsessed Students
q: When a student is only motivated by how an assignment will affect their grade, what that student is telling us is, "School is meaningless." It's "jump through X hoops to get Y treats so that someday, far away, I can do things that are actually important and meaningful." In terms of genuine motivation for learning, that's a big miss.

It is no fun to jump through hoops to get artificial prizes. It is no fun to experience high school as nothing more than four years of GPA-building so that I can go to the college I want to go to, or to experience middle school as staying on the honor roll so I don't get grounded, or what have you. Such conditions are antagonistic toward our students' souls.

Both kinds of systems reduce student work into a letter or a number, and both systems, by existing, reinforce this idea that such a reduction is a sensible thing to do. So whichever grading system your school uses, remind yourself that what you're seeing in a grade-obsessed student is a pretty logical and even responsible response to the system.

I bet I say some version of "master the material" 500 times per class period per school year. I need to repeat it this often because it's a definition of success most secondary students are unfamiliar with.

Foggy definitions of success — or unhelpful ones that focus just on grades — are a leading cause of anti-Efficacy in students. This is why "Define Success: Wisely, Early, and Often" is one of only 10 strategies I unpack in The Will to Learn. It's a mission-critical teacher practice.

t: The Effect of Teacher Coaching on Instruction and Achievement: A Meta-Analysis of the Causal Evidence esearchgate.net/publication/323344838_The_Effect_of_Teacher_Coaching_on_Instruction_and_Achie
q: Combining results across 60 studies that employ causal research designs, we find pooled effect sizes of 0.49 standard deviations (SD) on instruction and 0.18 SD on achievement.

Effective coaching is characterized by several critical features that teachers should seek out in PD opportunities: it must be individualized (one-on-one), intensive (interactions at least every couple of weeks), sustained (over a semester or year), context-specific (in their own classroom), and focused on deliberate practice of discrete skills.
Teachers should note that large-scale programs show significantly smaller effects than small efficacy trials.
Effective coaching requires substantial teacher buy-in and relational trust, which is challenging to achieve if the program is mandatory or tied to evaluation.

For coaching to be effective, its quality and focus may be more important than the actual number of contact hours (dosage), meaning teachers should prioritise the rigour and relevance of interactions over sheer frequency.
Modest changes in practice are unlikely to result in student impacts.

t: Leaders Must Ask for Sacrifice or All They Get Is Compliance
q: Achieving sizeable results and extraordinary outcomes normally requires great sacrifice.
when leaders ask team members to sacrifice for the greater good, it becomes a delicate calculus .
That’s why good leaders never presume or expect sacrifice. They always ask for it.
They give up their own comforts before asking others to give up theirs.
Remember, sacrifice can never be compelled. It can only be given freely, or it is compliance, not sacrifice.

t: Strong Leaders Always Defend Others From Unfair Criticism
q: good leaders...maintain a sharp eye for derogatory remarks, putdowns, and unfair feedback directed at their team members.
When team members know from experience that a leader will step in to set the record straight...they will be willing to walk through walls for that leader.
Leaders can always defend the quality and value of the person.
A leader can admire the person without condoning specific behavior.
Any slap directed at a team member becomes a slap aimed at them. They strike back in a supportive but professional way.

t: Research Bite #44: Practice Does Not Make Perfect – Experimental Evidence on the Effectiveness of Coaching Beginning Teachers
q: This research paper investigates the effectiveness of coaching versus self-reflection for beginning teachers using mixed-reality simulations.
coaching consistently improved behavioral redirection skills across all sites
Directive coaching from an expert is significantly more effective than self-reflection for improving teaching skills in simulated practice.

This study makes clear that the more typical teacher preparation approach of reflecting on one's simulated practice will not help beginning teachers in the same ways as coaching and directive feedback from an expert
its impact on content-focused feedback was more variable, particularly for teachers in an alternative route program.
Novices often struggle to effectively self-reflect without external support or guidance, potentially lacking the schema to identify areas for improvement or overestimating their own abilities.

t: Create Internal Certifications for Team Members to Showcase Their Skills
q: When thoughtfully designed and instilled with rigor, Certifications provide tangible evidence of skill achievement.
The good news is that savvy leaders can create their own , sometimes with even more value than external accreditations.
those who are considered masters in the role can help to identify the core skills and practices that define high competence.
By engaging in the Certification process and attaining its endorsement, they achieve a personal satisfaction that energizes their learning
Oddly enough, Certification creates as much self-recognition as it offers social proof.

t: Initiate New Relationships by Finding a Common Connection
q: establishing a relationship through a “cold” one-way introduction is among the scariest and most difficult of human tasks.
Common connections put people at ease, offer social proof that the other party is safe to speak with
The good news is that social media now makes it easy to learn of mutual connections you had no idea existed.
The shared reference point is a great launching pad into other points of shared interest.
be sure to follow up with the person you reference. They will be pleased to know that the circle of relationships has been expanded.

t: Making the Office More Attractive to Team Members
q: Team members have come to view the flexibility of remote work as a reward and are reluctant to give it up.
Consider JP Morgan’s massive $3 billion investment in their New York City Headquarters as a case in point.
The newly constructed 60-story fortress includes a Michelin-starred vegan restaurant, a café serving protein shakes from an Airstream trailer
While lighting, artwork, and issues of décor can make a critical difference, it is comfort and convenience that matter most.
Even small investments in convenience can make a major difference. People like to work where they are most comfortable.

t: Why Your Classroom Routines Must Be Longer
q: You can combine two or more classroom routines into one or add steps to an existing routine. Either way, longer routines are better.
Your students need goals to accomplish. They need targets, lined up one after the other, to shoot at.
Boredom, low-bar standards, laziness, and indifference are the death knell of healthy classroom culture.
You must ensure your students maintain a level of focus throughout the entirety of their time with you, whether for one period or the whole day.
Hard work, good performance, and motivation all transfer. And so do their opposites. Therefore, if you accept mindless and sloppy routines, student work will suffer.
The same old, same old just doesn’t work anymore. Times have changed. You must adjust or this job will crush you, as it’s currently doing to so many teachers.

t: The Dual Coding Delusion
q: But as with so many ideas in education, what began as an elegant theory has metastasised into caricature.

Crucially, though, dual coding was never intended as an instruction manual. It was a descriptive theory of how information might be represented in memory, not a prescriptive guide to classroom practice.
In classroom life, dual coding has been simplified into add pictures to your teaching. This is roughly equivalent to saying that because protein builds muscle, you should eat steak for every meal.
If words and images pull in different directions, or if graphics are merely decorative, the extra channel becomes noise rather than signal.
Teachers, in an earnest bid to dual code, raid sites like the Noun Project, pasting generic icons as if clip-art could stand in for cognition.
The danger of over-simplified dual coding lies not in using visuals, but in forgetting what they’re for.

t: Lesson Planning Is Not the Basics: Why We're Training Teachers Backwards
q: Planning is not the basics. Planning is the be all and end all, the Alpha and Omega, the Everest of teaching.
The basics are lesson starts, behaviour routines, transitions, scanning the room, moving to each part of the room, vocal control, body language, gestures and non verbal intervention.
When I started teaching, more than 95% of my time was spent on one thing: planning lessons from scratch.

Think about the math for a moment. A full-time teacher needs to plan 4-5 one-hour lessons per day. If a truly good lesson planned from scratch takes, conservatively, one hour, you are signing up for 4-5 hours of planning every single day.

We are, as David Didau suggests, inviting stupidity in. We violate the core tenet of Explicit Instruction - that teaching should be scaffolded to reduce cognitive load - by handing the biggest, most complex task (full planning) to the least experienced person.
Let’s focus our newest colleagues on mastering the performance of teaching, not the production of resources. Give them the plan, and watch them become expert teachers faster.

t: Leading a Highly Emotional Colleague
q: these colleagues seem hard-wired to respond intensely to all kinds of situations that wouldn’t bother many others.
Good leaders don’t try to “fix” or change emotional team members.
Scads of research confirm that giving emotions a label lessens their intensity.
High emotionality clouds judgment, slows down decision-making, and amplifies opinions and viewpoints.
Good leaders remember there is a genuine honesty in emotions that is as refreshing as it is uncomfortable at times.

t: A Multi-Stranded Math Curriculum
q: I’ve always felt like the math curriculum moves too fast. I teach topic A, and I know students could use some more practice to consolidate their understanding. But we have to move on to topic B.
Math is sequential. New topics build on earlier ones. But math also isn’t one giant staircase.
Four of the six units are sequenced a bit like before, though now there’s more time for each unit. The other two units stretch in parallel through the entire year.
An English teacher would never create artificial divisions where unit one focuses only on vocabulary, and then doesn't do any work on vocabulary the rest of the year.
This approach to curriculum does not work if you are set on having a single objective for each lesson.
I learned about this idea from the book Direct Instruction: A Practitioner’s Handbook.

t: 3-Read Friday #89: Lesson Planning, Dual Coding, and Multi-Stranded Curriculum
q: Dr Dario is my new favourite Substacker. Read this post for a compelling argument for why we need to give novice teachers high-quality, already planned lessons.
When Dual Coding was all the rage a few years ago, every PowerPoint slide had to be accompanied by a visual representation, no matter how tenuous.
David dives into Dual Coding research to examine when integrating text and images is useful.
One for the maths geeks. Dylan outlines how he has changed the format of his scheme of work this year, why he did so, and offers practical tips for anyone wishing to try this approach too.
Before we begin, you may want to check out my brand-new 16-part book series, The Tips for Teachers guide to. Book 7 on Responsive Teaching is now available.

t: Sorry, I Can't Help You Right Now
q: Presuming a team or organization will naturally develop a highly collaborative spirit of working together doesn’t make it so.
the most senior, tenured, experienced, and influential team members are just as willing to lend a hand to a junior colleague as they are to their leader.
Developing such a collective team spirit almost always starts with an explicit expectation by the leader.
Research confirms that teams high in collaboration are more engaged, more productive, more innovative, and more adaptive to change.
When those too busy or important to support others learn from you that their behavior is unacceptable, they quickly get in line and conform to the group norm.

t: Are You a Passive, Aggressive, or Assertive Teacher?
q: Because you are often not saying what you mean, you don't look like you mean what you say.
You are so intent on being right that you don't really hear what others are saying, even when you ask them a direct question.
No problem stating how you feel or what you think, but you tend to state these things at the expense of the feelings and thoughts of others
Tending to humiliate others without knowing it through things like sarcasm and humor

If you're like me, you'll notice that all three styles pop up in you throughout a given school day. Us human beings are complicated! But you'll likely find that one style tends to predominate, and this is something worth reflecting on. The goal is the assertive style, which closely aligns with a warm and authoritative teacher presence.

t: Your Leadership Role Opens Up New Conversations if You Let It
q: Smart leaders open doors that many other leaders don’t even realize exist.
The title, authority, and influence any leader enjoys make them interesting to other leaders.
a VP of marketing at a tech startup can connect with a VP of marketing at nearly any other company
These external relationships offer something no one in your internal network can match: a fresh perspective, different approaches
Your leadership role is a passport to conversations that weren’t available to you before.

t: Student-Generated Examples in the Learning of Mathematics https://tipsforteachers.co.uk/research-student-generated-examples-in-the-learning-of-mathematics/ -- original paper: https://www.researchgate.net/publication/251513468_Student-generated_examples_in_
q: This research article investigates common difficulties students face in mathematics, specifically their understanding of theorems and the use of examples.
The authors propose that encouraging students to generate their own examples, especially boundary cases, improves comprehension and retention.
When students are taught techniques as a set of mechanical manipulations, they may not see the creative problem-solving aspects of the technique.

The authors discuss several strategies for helping students appreciate a particular mathematical example, especially a boundary example that shows why constraints are required in a definition or theorem. Students sometimes dismiss these examples as pathologies.

Any technique which yields answers illustrates ways to construct mathematical objects. Solving a first order linear differential equation, finding an integral, disentangling eigenvalues and eigenvectors for a matrix, and changing basis are all examples of constructing an object with specified properties.
Thus constructing mathematical objects is something students have seen and done a great deal of, yet for the most part they are unaware of it in these terms.

t: Shame and Motivation Don't Mix
q: A person who does a thing — who even does it well — is not necessarily a person who cares about what they've done. Instead, the person can be driven by care for the carrots or the sticks. This, in my observation, is the condition of most folks who do well in our secondary schools today.

What I'd like to put forth in this book is that such a person, regardless of grades or achievement, is actually a poorly motivated human soul. They'll do work, but it won't be done from the fullness of their agency. And so, eventually, they'll find themselves alienated from the fundamental goodness of learning. They'll lose the sensory capacity for tasting and seeing that an education is good.
What I'm writing about today is the reality that being poorly motivated isn't something anyone should be ashamed of. And we should never cast aspersion on a student who is poorly motivated in school.
Students want to want to learn. They'd much prefer the state of motivation to the state of apathy. We are all alike in this preference.
The thing to do is treat them like a human being brimming with dignity and do the kinds of things that can help the seeds of true care grow. You can tend the soil. You can water and weed.
Shame is a terrible and counterproductive tool. It is also a deceitful tool — it seems like it works sometimes, but what it actually does is poisons the soul.

t: Don’t Cast Team Obligations as Goals During the Review and Planning Process
q: One of the most common errors leaders make in the goal-setting process is to classify everyday obligations and commitments as goals to achieve rather than as responsibilities to uphold
Casting everyday responsibilities as goals reduces accountability for being a productive team member.
It sends the message that the obligations and commitments of being a team member are optional or elective.
This pass-or-fail mentality sets the standard for all team members.
In that case, have the discussion to meet the standard, but don’t present them as goals. A great team culture depends on it.

t: Research Bite #43: Examining the Academic Effects of Cross-age Tutoring
q: This meta-analysis synthesises 32 studies on the academic effects of cross-age tutoring, an educational model pairing older tutors with younger tutees.
The research found a small to moderate positive impact on academic outcomes for both tutors and tutees.
This model yields small to moderate positive academic effects for both the younger tutees (0.33) and, notably, the older student tutors (0.39).
Tutors engage in self-explanation and verbalisation, which helps them convert implicit knowledge into explicit knowledge, enhancing their own comprehension and retention.
high heterogeneity (I² values) indicates that unexamined variables may influence outcomes, suggesting a need for more detailed reporting in future research.
The meta-analysis revealed a small to moderate positive effect of cross-age tutoring on academic outcomes for both tutors and tutees

t: Protecting the Team by Saying ‘No’ Upstream
q: Shielding the team and team members from unwanted noise preserves focus and improves morale.
Leaders above are often the source of noise and distraction. They can direct work, create unnecessary urgency
Saying “No” can delay leaders upstream, allowing the team to maintain its focus and avoid being pulled in multiple directions.
protecting the team can also require leaders to run interference with powerful internal stakeholders, such as compliance, risk, legal, and human resources.
Good leaders stand in the line of fire so their team members can stand for what is most important.

t: Getting a Head Start
q: He believed that even a small company could compete with the largest consumer product companies if it had the best product and could get a head start.
Taylor spent $12 million to purchase 100 million pump dispensers from the only two U.S. manufacturers at the time.
The Softsoap brand quickly dominated the market and established itself as a household name before the competitors could retaliate.
Getting a head start is an essential leadership strategy in any organization or team, no matter what the idea, service, product, or initiative.
When people and resources are behind you, getting a head start is relatively easy.
